newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industrial insurance prices to fall - broker.
newsitem.headline: German industrial insurance prices to fall - broker.

text.p: German industrial insurers are prepared to grant wide-ranging price cuts, particularly for risks with high fire protection, said Paul Grothaus, a manager at German insurance broker Jauch & Huebener.

Grothaus said at an industry meeting on Friday that insurers had until recently pushed through massive price increases especially for so-called top risks with insured sums of more than one billion marks and 250 million marks for petrochemical plants.
This followed "catastrophic losses" in the early 1990s.

"In some cases insurers overdid the rate restoration," said Grothaus. "Our customers also did not understand the fact that a good loss record and preventive measures were often not adequately rewarded. This will now change."

Grothaus cited several reasons for the price cuts -- higher capacity from reinsurers, the sometimes spectacular move of 25 to 30 top risks to international markets and the end of the consortium commissions (Kokos), where insurers for many years jointly set prices for top risks.

In addition, major industrial insurers such as Allianz and Gerling have developed their own fire tariffs and no longer adhere to tariff recommendations of the property and casualty insurers' federation, Verband der Schadenversicherer.
According to Grothaus, industrial fire insurance is likely to return underwriting losses in 1997, as it is doing in 1996.
At the same meeting, a leading insurance buyer said that the new industrial fire tariff of the Allianz group was very difficult to handle.

Klaus Schulze-Weslarn, a director of the chemical group Henkel and head of its central insurance department, said it had a long-standing relationship with Allianz unit Frankfurter Allianz but was having difficulties.

"We have longstanding connections with Allianz group member Frankfurter Allianz, which has been our leading insurer for more than 50 years. We gave them a chance to test the new tariff. The test proved impractical. It took three days to rate one single building in our Holthausen works," he said.
Schulze-Weslarn said Henkel was spending 50 million marks annually on insurance premiums, 14 million of that in Europe.

Henkel reported 1995 global revenues of 14.2 billion marks. All risks that could affect the group's balance sheet were placed through the central insurance department, including property, loss-of-profit (business interruption) and liability.

He said international industrial groups needed a single insurance philosophy, for example on deductibles. Henkel's subsidiaries had a 20,000 marks deductible for each claim, plus a major deductible carried by the holding company.

Henkel also needed to know the relationships between its primary insurers and reinsurers. Such a company also needed to have an international presence, an adequate structure and effective links between the centre and each country, he said.
Claims handling had to be done at a local level, but under central control, he said.
